knockouts.question: Do you currently hold an active, unencumbered California RN license?
knockouts.pass_if: Yes, active and unencumbered in California. A license from another state only, or one pending California endorsement with a date, is 'unclear'.
knockouts.clarify: Is that a California license, and is it active right now?

knockouts.question: Is your BLS certification current?
knockouts.pass_if: Yes, current BLS. ACLS is a plus, not required.
knockouts.fail_if: No BLS and no plan to renew before start.

knockouts.question: This role is nights, three twelve-hour shifts a week, with every third weekend. Does that schedule work for you?
knockouts.pass_if: Yes, or yes with a minor constraint the team could accommodate.
knockouts.fail_if: Cannot work nights or weekends at all.
knockouts.clarify: Is that a hard no on nights, or something we could work around?

anchors.1: Cannot describe a specific deteriorating patient, or describes waiting without acting.
anchors.2: Generic answer ('I'd call the doctor') with no assessment steps or specifics.
anchors.3: A real example with assessment and escalation, but vague on cues, timing, or outcome.
anchors.4: Specific cues (vitals trend, mental status), a clear escalation path (charge nurse, rapid response, provider), and an outcome.
anchors.5: Specific early-warning cues, prioritized actions while escalating, structured handoff (e.g. SBAR), outcome, and what they learned.

anchors.1: Dismissive of the patient or family, or no example.
anchors.2: States they 'explain things' with no example or technique.
anchors.3: A real example of calming or informing a patient or family, with limited detail on what they said or did.
anchors.4: Specific words or actions used, checks understanding (teach-back or similar), stays within scope.
anchors.5: Handles a hard conversation (upset family, refusal of care) with empathy, clear boundaries, and appropriate escalation; describes the result.

anchors.1: Blames others, or describes leaving tasks undone without communicating.
anchors.2: Says they are a team player with no example.
anchors.3: An example of helping or asking for help on a busy shift, light on how priorities were set.
anchors.4: Describes prioritizing a heavy assignment, communicating with the charge nurse, and delegating appropriately to CNAs.
anchors.5: Clear prioritization logic, safe delegation, closed-loop communication, and how they supported a colleague without dropping their own patients.

anchors.1: No EHR experience and no sense of documentation timing.
anchors.2: Names an EHR but cannot describe their charting routine.
anchors.3: Uses an EHR daily; describes charting at the end of shift.
anchors.4: Charts in near real time, names what they document after a change in condition.
anchors.5: Real-time charting habits, accurate late-entry practice, and how documentation supports handoff and safety.

question_bank.question: Tell me about a time a patient's condition started to get worse during your shift. What did you notice, and what did you do?
question_bank.probe: What was the first thing that tipped you off, and who did you call?
question_bank.short: Can you walk me through one time a patient got worse on your shift?

question_bank.question: Tell me about a time you had to calm down an upset patient or family member. What did you say?
question_bank.probe: How did you know they understood you?
question_bank.short: Any time you had to calm down an upset patient or family?

question_bank.question: Think of your busiest night shift. How did you decide what to do first, and how did you work with the rest of the team?
question_bank.probe: Did you hand anything off to a CNA or ask the charge nurse for help?
question_bank.short: On a really busy shift, how do you decide what comes first?

question_bank.question: Which EHR have you used, and when during a shift do you usually chart?
question_bank.probe: What do you make sure to document when a patient's condition changes?
question_bank.short: Which charting system have you used?

faq.q: pay, salary, hourly rate, differential, sign-on bonus
faq.a: I can't speak to pay, but a recruiter will go over compensation with you directly.
It's nights, three twelve-hour shifts a week, seven p.m. to seven a.m., with every third weekend.
It's a thirty-two bed medical-surgical unit. I don't have exact ratios; the team can share those.

faq.q: next steps, timeline, when will I hear back
faq.a: The recruiting team reviews every screen within a few business days and will reach out by email.

faq.q: start date, when can I start
faq.a: I can't commit to a start date; the recruiter will discuss timing with you.
I don't have benefit details, but I'll note that you asked and the recruiter will follow up.
It's at the main Riverside campus in San Francisco, California. I don't have parking details; I'll note the question.

avoid: age, family, religion, national origin, disability, pregnancy, or any protected characteristic
